tagline: The shortest and fastest of the four Gospels: the story of Jesus, the Son of God, who came to serve and to give his life, told at a run toward the cross and an empty tomb.
overview:
Mark is the shortest of the four Gospels, the books that tell the story of Jesus' ministry, death, and resurrection. It opens with a single line that works as a title, “This is the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God” (1:1), and then moves at speed. There is no birth story and no long sermon like Matthew's Sermon on the Mount. John the Baptist appears in the wilderness, Jesus is baptized and tested, and within a few verses he is in Galilee calling fishermen, casting out unclean spirits, healing the sick, forgiving sins, and colliding with the religious authorities.

The book turns on a question: who is this man? Crowds, demons, disciples, and opponents all try to answer it. Halfway through, at Caesarea Philippi, Peter says, “You are the Christ” (8:29), and at once Jesus begins to teach that the Son of Man must suffer, be killed, and rise again (8:31). From there the story walks the road to Jerusalem, where Jesus enters the city, confronts the temple, is arrested, tried, and crucified. The first human being in Mark to call him the Son of God is a Roman centurion at the foot of the cross, at the moment of his death (15:39). The book closes with women at an empty tomb, told that he has risen.

Mark matters because most scholars judge it the earliest written Gospel, and because it refuses to separate who Jesus is from what he suffered. Its Jesus has authority over storms, disease, and demons, and he uses that authority on the way to a cross. The sentence many readers take as the book's center says it plainly: “For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many” (10:45).
author:
Like the other Gospels, Mark does not name its author in the text. The title According to Mark was attached in the early church, and the tradition behind it is early. Papias, a bishop of Hierapolis in Asia Minor writing in the early second century, is reported by the church historian Eusebius (in his Ecclesiastical History, 3.39) to have said, on the authority of an older teacher he calls the elder, that Mark had been Peter's interpreter and wrote down accurately, though not in order, what he remembered of the things the Lord said and did. Later writers, including Irenaeus near the end of the second century, repeat and expand the link between Mark and Peter.

The Mark of this tradition is usually identified with John Mark of the New Testament: the son of a Mary whose Jerusalem house was a meeting place for the church (Acts 12:12), a companion of Paul and Barnabas who turned back partway through their first mission trip (Acts 13:13), the cause of a sharp split between them (Acts 15:37-39), and later a trusted coworker of Paul (Colossians 4:10, 2 Timothy 4:11). First Peter 5:13 sends greetings from “my son Mark,” which fits the Petrine link. Many scholars accept the tradition in broad terms; Richard Bauckham, in Jesus and the Eyewitnesses (2006), argued at length that Mark rests on Peter's testimony. Others doubt that Papias knew what he claimed, or think the name Mark was common enough that the identification with John Mark is uncertain. What nearly everyone agrees on is that the author wrote in plain, vivid Greek, knew Aramaic (he keeps Aramaic phrases and translates them), and wrote for readers who needed Jewish customs explained.
date:
Most scholars date Mark between the late 60s and the early 70s AD, and the debate within that range turns largely on chapter 13, where Jesus predicts the destruction of the temple. Some read the chapter as written during the Jewish revolt against Rome (AD 66-70), when the temple was threatened but still standing, and note that it does not describe the city's fall in the kind of detail one might expect after the event. Others place it just after AD 70, holding that the destruction stands behind the text. Scholars who take Jesus' prophecy as genuine predictive speech see no need to date the book after the event on that ground.

The early tradition is divided: Irenaeus placed the writing after the deaths of Peter and Paul, which tradition sets in Rome under Nero in the mid 60s, while Clement of Alexandria said Mark wrote while Peter was still preaching in Rome. A minority of scholars argues for a considerably earlier date, in the 40s or 50s.

Mark's date is tied to the question of how the first three Gospels (the Synoptics, so called because they can be seen together) relate. Most scholars today hold that Mark was written first and that Matthew and Luke each used it, since they reproduce most of its content and often its wording and order. A minority defends other views: some, following the church tradition that goes back to Augustine, hold that Matthew came first, and the Two-Gospel hypothesis, revived by William Farmer in the 1960s, holds that Mark drew on both Matthew and Luke. On the majority view, Mark's date also shapes the dating of Matthew and Luke.
setting:
Jesus' ministry took place in the late 20s or early 30s AD, in a land ruled by Rome. Galilee in the north was governed by Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, while Judea and Jerusalem were under a Roman governor, Pontius Pilate, from about AD 26 to 36. The Jerusalem temple, rebuilt on a grand scale by Herod the Great, was the center of Jewish worship and was run by the high priest and the chief priestly families, who answered to Rome. Pharisees (a lay renewal movement devoted to careful keeping of the law and its traditions), scribes (experts in the law), and Sadducees (the priestly aristocracy) all appear as Jesus' questioners and opponents.

Mark's first readers are less certain. The tradition places them in Rome, and the book has features that fit: it explains Jewish washing customs (7:3-4), translates Aramaic words, and uses several Latin loanwords, including one that explains a Jewish coin in terms of Roman money (12:42). Its steady attention to suffering and to faithfulness under pressure would have spoken directly to Christians in Rome after Nero's persecution following the great fire of AD 64. Other scholars propose Syria or Galilee as the setting. On any view the readers were largely Gentile believers who needed to understand both the Jewish world of Jesus and the cost of following him.
purpose: Mark calls his book a gospel, meaning good news, and in the Roman world that word could announce a victory or the accession of an emperor. Mark uses it for the news that God's kingdom has come near in Jesus (1:14-15). The book is written to tell who Jesus is, the Christ and the Son of God, and to show that his identity cannot be understood apart from the cross. It also shapes disciples. The Twelve in Mark are slow, frightened, and often wrong, and the book presents their failures honestly, which would have both warned and comforted readers who were themselves being tested. Jesus' call to deny oneself, take up the cross, and follow (8:34) is addressed to every reader, not only to the first followers.
story: Mark picks up the story where the Old Testament's prophets left it. It begins with a quotation from Isaiah and Malachi about a messenger preparing the way of the Lord, so that John the Baptist steps into Israel's long hope for God's return and the renewal of his people. Jesus then announces that the time is fulfilled. The book ends at the empty tomb with a promise that the risen Jesus is going ahead of his disciples into Galilee, which points forward to the church's witness in Acts and the letters. Matthew and Luke retell much of Mark's account with material of their own, and John tells the same story from a different angle.
christ: Mark is entirely about Christ, and it builds its portrait from two sides. On one side is authority: Jesus forgives sins, which his opponents say only God can do (2:7), calms the sea, raises a dead girl, and speaks with the authority of Israel's God. On the other is suffering: three times he predicts his death and resurrection (8:31, 9:31, 10:33-34), and each time the disciples misunderstand. Mark holds these together. The Son of God is recognized fully only at the cross, and Jesus' usual name for himself, the Son of Man, draws on Daniel 7's figure who receives everlasting dominion while also being the one who gives his life as a ransom. The church confesses on this ground that Jesus is truly God and truly man, crucified for sinners and bodily raised.
reading:
Read Mark in one sitting if you can; it takes about as long as a film, and its force comes from its pace. Watch the word translated “immediately,” which appears more than forty times and drives the action forward. Notice Mark's habit of sandwiching one story inside another (for example, Jairus's daughter and the bleeding woman in chapter 5), where each story explains the other. Watch the commands to silence, where Jesus tells people and demons not to make him known; since William Wrede's study of 1901 this has been called the messianic secret, and interpreters still debate what it means. Most readers see it as Jesus' refusal to be taken for the wrong kind of messiah before the cross made his meaning clear.

The ending needs a note. The oldest complete Greek manuscripts, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus from the fourth century, end the book at 16:8, with the women fleeing from the tomb in fear. Most later manuscripts include 16:9-20, the longer ending, and it was known by the late second century, since Irenaeus cites it. One Old Latin manuscript has a brief shorter ending instead, and several Greek manuscripts carry both. Most scholars conclude that 16:9-20 was added early by another hand, drawing on material found in the other Gospels and Acts; a minority defends it as original. Among those who think it was added, some hold that Mark meant to end at 16:8, leaving the reader with the promise of Galilee and the silence of the women, while others think the original ending was lost. Most modern Bibles print the longer ending with a note, and readers can treat it with the care that the evidence calls for.

structure.title: The beginning of the gospel
structure.summary: John the Baptist prepares the way, Jesus is baptized and hears the Father's voice, and the Spirit drives him into the wilderness to be tested.

structure.title: Authority in Galilee
structure.summary: Jesus announces the kingdom, calls disciples, heals, casts out spirits, and forgives sins, and a string of controversies ends with his opponents plotting against him.

structure.title: Parables, power, and rejection
structure.summary: Jesus appoints the Twelve, teaches in parables, and shows authority over the sea, demons, disease, and death, but is rejected in his hometown.

structure.title: Bread and blindness
structure.summary: The Twelve are sent out, John is executed, and Jesus feeds great crowds and walks on the sea, while the disciples struggle to understand.

structure.title: On the road to the cross
structure.summary: Peter confesses Jesus as the Christ, and on the way to Jerusalem Jesus predicts his death three times and teaches what following him costs. The section is bracketed by two healings of blind men, one just before it (8:22-26) and one at its close (10:46-52).

structure.title: Jesus in Jerusalem
structure.summary: Jesus enters the city, clears the temple, debates the authorities, and on the Mount of Olives foretells the temple's destruction and the coming of the Son of Man.

structure.title: The passion
structure.summary: Jesus is anointed, shares the Passover meal, prays in Gethsemane, is betrayed, tried, denied by Peter, crucified, and buried.

structure.title: The empty tomb
structure.summary: The women find the tomb empty and hear that Jesus has risen and is going ahead of the disciples into Galilee. Verses 9-20, the longer ending, are absent from the oldest manuscripts.

themes.title: The kingdom of God has come near
themes.body: Jesus' first words in Mark announce that the time is fulfilled and God's kingdom is near (1:15). The kingdom is God's reign breaking into a world held by sickness, evil spirits, and sin. Jesus' healings and exorcisms are signs of that reign, and his parables in chapter 4 explain that it grows from hidden, small beginnings to a great harvest.

themes.title: Who is this man?
themes.body: The question of Jesus' identity runs through the whole book. The disciples ask it after the storm (4:41), Herod wonders about it, and Jesus asks it himself at Caesarea Philippi (8:29). The reader knows the answer from 1:1, and the drama lies in watching the characters struggle toward it, often getting the words right and the meaning wrong.

themes.title: The way of the cross
themes.body: After Peter's confession, every prediction of the passion is followed by teaching on discipleship: deny yourself, be the servant of all, and follow Jesus to the cross. Mark insists that the Messiah's path runs through suffering and that his followers' path does too. This was not abstract for readers who faced persecution.

themes.title: Failure and grace
themes.body: Mark does not flatter the disciples. They misunderstand, argue about greatness, fall asleep in Gethsemane, and flee at the arrest, and Peter denies Jesus three times. Yet the angel's message at the tomb names Peter in particular (16:7). The book offers hope not in the disciples' strength but in the faithfulness of the one who goes ahead of them.

keyChapters.why: The title verse, John's preaching, Jesus' baptism, and the announcement of the kingdom set the terms for the whole book.
The parables of the kingdom and the stilling of the storm show how God's reign grows and raise the question of who Jesus is.
Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi and the first passion prediction are the hinge of the Gospel.
Jesus teaches the way of the servant and gives the book's central statement of why he came, to give his life as a ransom for many.
The Olivet discourse foretells the temple's destruction and the coming of the Son of Man and calls disciples to watchfulness.
The crucifixion, where the centurion confesses Jesus as the Son of God, is the climax of Mark's portrait.
The empty tomb and the message of the resurrection close the book, and the question of its ending is best understood here.
